newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Besieged Albania government faces fresh protests.
newsitem.headline: Besieged Albania government faces fresh protests.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha called for calm as fiery protests against collapsing pyramid investment schemes swept the nation and the opposition Socialists vowed to press ahead with a protest rally on Sunday.

"I call on all citizens to cool down and I assure them that we're doing our utmost to strike the right solution so that (investors) can retrieve their money as soon as possible," a weary Berisha told state television.

Berisha's right-wing Democratic government has come under heavy pressure as investors, angry at losing their life savings in the murky schemes, turned to force and directed their ire against the authorities in Europe's poorest country.
Angry crowds set fire to government buildings in the southern towns of Lushnje and Berat on Saturday and state television reported disturbances in six other towns in the region.
A crowd of about 5,000 people set upon Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu, the Democratic Party chairman, in Lushnje, 80 km (55 miles) south of Tirana.

Shehu, blood pouring down his face, took refuge in the town's soccer stadium and escaped after five hours under cover of an electricity black-out, witnesses said. State television reported that he was on his way back to Tirana.

In Berat, 40 km (25 miles) south of Lushnje, demonstrators set fire to the town hall, a police station, the prosecutor's office and court buildings, the television said. The buildings were still smouldering late on Saturday.

Berisha held a crisis meeting of parliamentary parties at the presidential palace in Tirana and said after more than two hours of talks that the government would do its utmost to ensure investors in the bankrupt schemes were not left empty-handed.
"I will make sure that eveybody gets their savings," he said, adding that depositors should remain patient and understand the enormity of the task of repaying them.
But the Socialists, reformed heirs to the communists who ruled Albania for half a century, said they would hold a rally in Tirana on Sunday to press their demand for the government's resignation.
"It is the people's right to protest peacefully against the government," said senior Socialist official Maqo Lakrori.

In Lushnje, protesters said they would take to the streets in their thousands again on Sunday and maintain a crippling blockade of the country's main north-south highway. "We will not lift the barricades," one demonstrator said.
The Socialists have boycotted parliament since a controversial general election last year and said they turned down an invitation from Berisha to attend his palace meeting.

The violence marked a serious escalation in two weeks of street protests by impoverished people who had poured their life savings into dubious pyramid investment schemes which offered huge returns for little outlay.

Berisha's Democrats, facing one of their biggest crises since ousting the former communists in a 1992 general election, have attempted to appease investors by banning the pyramid schemes and setting 20-year jail sentences for their operators.
But they have succeeded only in stoking investors' fury by freezing pyramid scheme funds and jailing their managers, depriving many people of their last hope of recovering their money.
